qs.q: A 10-year-old child sustains a blunt abdominal trauma during a sports match and is noted to have a ureteric injury at the pelviureteric junction. What is the underlying mechanical cause for this specific injury in children?
o: Direct compression of the ureter against the rigid 12th rib
The renal pelvis is congenitally narrowed and prone to shear
Avulsion due to rapid deceleration forces on a fixed renal hilum
The ureter is tensed over the hyperextended spine
qs.e: In children, blunt deceleration injuries can cause avulsion at the PUJ because the ureter is tensed over the hyperextended spine. Deceleration alone without the spinal hyperextension component is less specific to this pediatric PUJ mechanism.

qs.q: During an exploratory laparotomy for abdominal trauma, a surgeon notices clear fluid accumulating in the surgical field and an absence of efflux after administering indigo carmine. What injury should the surgeon immediately suspect?
qs.e: Intra-operative recognition of ureteric injury includes clear fluid in the field, a ureteric transection, or lack of efflux using methylene blue or indigo carmine tests. Bladder injuries do not test ureteric efflux of intravenous dye.

qs.q: A 17-year-old truck driver is involved in a collision. He incurs blunt force abdominal trauma. In response to this injury, cells in tissues of the abdomen are stimulated to enter the G1 phase of the cell cycle from the G0 phase. Which of the following cell types is most likely to remain in G0 following this injury?
qs.e: Skeletal and cardiac muscle cells do not typically proliferate in response to injury, and necrotic cells are replaced by connective tissue. Remaining striated muscle cells, however, can undergo hypertrophy.

qs.q: A 20-year-old healthy man undergoes splenectomy after blunt abdominal trauma causes a splenic hematoma. Following splenectomy, which peripheral blood morphologic finding is most likely to appear?
qs.e: After splenectomy, the spleen can no longer remove RBC inclusions such as Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear remnants) and Pappenheimer bodies (iron granules). These inclusions appear in circulating RBCs because the filtering function of the spleen is lost.
